title: Individual productivity tripled, but company delivery only went from 20 days to 17
dek: AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the short plank in the barrel isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform process and organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
why: A frontline CEO talks about building his own CEO AI, canceling weekly meetings, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and numbers are concrete, and the decision hub section in the second half is the most valuable.
who: CEOs, CTOs, and HR leaders at companies pushing AI adoption, especially managers trying to understand why individual productivity improved but the organization didn't get faster.
skip: The first 4 minutes of education-scenario setup can be fast-forwarded; go straight to the barrel short-plank case at 16:07.

points.h: Individual productivity tripled, delivery only sped up by three days
points.body: NetEase did a count last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing a design doc to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled to quintupled their personal efficiency, some tenfold. But for features of the same scope, the whole process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of 20 planks, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product manager planks shoot up fast, but some planks aren't people — they're process — and they haven't improved at all. So AI adoption has to clear three hurdles: cognition, applying it to individuals' short-range tasks, and transforming process and organization. The third is the hardest.

points.h: Cancel the weekly meeting: AI syncs information, humans only solve problems
points.body: Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. Weekly meetings usually serve three purposes: sync information, discover problems and opportunities, and make decisions. They used to run 2.5 hours a week, but the time spent on that meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepares materials layer by layer, and the information sync itself isn't done well, because no one listens attentively the whole time and may miss a sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agree on what information is needed, everyone fills in a template and stores it in the knowledge base, and AI scans and integrates it into a focused, interactive HTML report where people can leave comments and follow-up questions; an AI agent produces a list of problems and opportunities in advance, and human brains confirm and supplement; solving problems and making decisions move to dedicated meetings.

points.h: SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
points.body: Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, it just changes form — AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may really die, while genuinely good SaaS that has already entered a company's critical processes will only get better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. In the past, humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future, a large number of agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, audit APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs — call volume will far exceed the number and actions of humans, will increase enormously, and the more it's called the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that the Service itself is critical enough inside the company.

points.h: Distill top salespeople into skills and distribute them to everyone
points.body: Bosses have two headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is so strong that if they leave, what then? Previously there was no way; now you can distill or extract the actions, scripts, and behaviors of good salespeople into skills. Two uses: distribute them to other salespeople to use directly; and have AI turn elite salespeople into teachers to train ordinary salespeople. What training should distill isn't the salesperson — it's the customer: take the customer interaction data the salesperson has had — calls, WeChat, email — and have AI simulate various customers to train salespeople. Online sales is purely digital and on record; for offline sales, recommend or even require a recording card — after a visit, record a two-to-three-minute voice memo while memory is fresh, because salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is for managing them) but don't mind a recording card, since it's also useful for their own customer review.

points.h: Fewer middle managers, strong individuals lead agent legions back to the front line
points.body: Ruan Liang judges that middle managers will become fewer, but not necessarily be eliminated — rather they'll go to the front line, and the front line can also lead a bunch of agents. Middle managers with management responsibilities will become fewer; elite people with strong skills will become more numerous. He gives the example of an engineering team: previously social division of labor made software development more and more specialized — frontend, backend, algorithm, test engineers; in the last half year it has clearly reverted to full-stack, everyone becoming full-end engineers. In the future the organization will look more and more like a fractal structure: countless engineering capabilities are strong, one mother peak commands some engineering, and countless agents fight a battle. He imagines a future interview negotiation scenario: the candidate says I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, a summary of all my past experience and skills, and the premium the company pays might be some kind of OPC.

points.h: AI value formula: quality times time saved
points.body: Ruan Liang gives a formula referencing a paper: AI value = quality of AI completing the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at eight out of ten, AI also makes it at eight out of ten, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit time and you can calculate ROI. Prioritize four types of tasks for AI: time-consuming, high-frequency, unavoidable, and tasks where different people produce roughly the same result. Once calculated, you can immediately decide whether to use AI. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Claude, GPT) to prove the task can be done, solidify the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheap ones can too.

points.h: Token consumption leads by a landslide, output also leads by a landslide
points.body: NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work tasks into points with work value. By the AI era they found a group of people whose token consumption was astonishing, and whose work output and work value were also astonishing, forming a statistical pattern: people whose token consumption leads by a landslide are most likely building systems for themselves, saving their own work time and increasing thinking time, so their work quality and results also lead by a landslide. Many bosses worry about AI abuse causing waste; Ruan Liang's hot take is that truly excellent or elite people won't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through statistics they found elite colleagues don't waste. He also says small companies are more likely to fully embrace AI, because there are fewer organizational relationships, the boss uses it first, hierarchy is shallow, and the chain is short.

points.h: The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
points.body: Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base, and what really matters is the historical decision processes and decision bases. This year NetEase preserved historical decisions, incorporated them into the knowledge base, combined two types of knowledge to train an agent or skill, then fed back hundreds of original cases for the agent to judge, achieving over 90% accuracy. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater Associates gave researchers and analysts agents they built themselves, precipitating decision processes and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater did better was making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a person adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment action enters the next round of reinforcement, advancing with the times, equivalent to human-machine collaborative self-evolution.

quotes.text: Across our whole process, for software features of similar scope, from product requirement to launch, it only shortened from 20 days to 17 days.
The third and hardest hurdle to cross is actually transforming the process — your organization. Once you transform the process, it inevitably means transforming the organization.
A two-and-a-half-hour meeting — it's impossible to be that focused every second; that would take a god.
Middle managers with management responsibilities will become fewer, but elite people with strong skills should become more numerous.
If your token consumption leads by a landslide, your work quality and work results are also most likely leading by a landslide.
Sometimes it's not that the boss wants to push and can push — because many organizations have ten thousand reasons to make sure this thing doesn't get done.
